accuracy.evidence: Checked against NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory and National Weather Service lightning pages and the Met Office: charge separation by collisions between small ice crystals (positive, carried up) and heavier graupel (negative, lower in the cloud); lightning heats air to about 30,000 °C (NWS: 50,000 °F), several times the Sun's surface (about 5,500 °C); thunder is the rapid expansion of heated air; sound travels about 343 m/s, so about 3 seconds per km (Met Office rule; NWS uses 5 seconds a mile); lightning often, not always, strikes the tallest object; buildings and hard-topped metal cars are safe, trees and open fields are not. 'Often' is used rather than 'always' throughout.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented misconceptions: thunder as clouds colliding (predict, heat-step buttons, challenge 'bump'), thunder happening after lightning (challenge 'later', practice p1), reading seconds as kilometres or multiplying by 3 (race-step feedback, challenge 'nine' and 'times', mastery m5), sheltering under a tree or in an open field (safe-step feedback, challenge 'tree' and 'field'), and lightning as fire (challenge 'fire'). The adult text also names the same-place-twice and rubber-tyres myths.

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab is built on this topic's own mechanism: ice collisions separate plus and minus charge, the charge has to build before it can jump, the spark goes to the taller tree, the bolt heats the air into a pressure ring, and a sped-up flash-to-bang count gives the distance. gate_lab_distinct passed (under 30% overlap with every flagship lab, including flagfade and flagwxinst).

lab_teaches.evidence: Learners see the plus charges rise and minus sink with each bump before the text names it, find that Spark fails until the meter is full, watch the strike pick the tree over the house, see the air ring expand before naming thunder, and work out 9 seconds = 3 km from their own count before the 3-seconds-per-km rule is confirmed.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options, each tested in the lab: small ice goes down (it visibly rises), lightning hits the house roof or the grass (it hits the taller tree), thunder is clouds crashing or rain (the air ring and BOOM come from the heated air).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Eight rotating questions with 13 specific feedback messages: fire, sunlight, clouds bumping, rain, thunder later, eyes faster than ears, seconds-as-km, multiplying instead of dividing, tree, field, lowest place, only water, and a growing count meaning the storm moves away.

readability.evidence: validate_lessons.py passed the learner readability limits (kid at most 6.5, adult at most 9.5). Kid paragraphs use short sentences, explain 'charges' and compare lightning to a door-handle shock; on-canvas text is short labels and the buttons say exactly what they do.

no_filler.evidence: gate_content passed the filler patterns and the 12% duplicate limit against all other lessons (700 and 876 only mention thunder in one item each). Every paragraph carries a mechanism, a number or a safety rule.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 px (Android, 2x) at the end of every task in light and dark themes, plus gate_browser on iPhone 13 and 1200 px desktop. The first pass had the storm cloud covering the step banner, the charge meter under the bolt, the heat rings over the banner with clipped labels and empty safe-place boxes; the cloud is now sized to fit under the banner, the meter sits to the right, the rings are smaller with labels underneath, and each place has a picture.

accessibility.evidence: gate_browser passed: axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13, all five tasks complete with Show me, no console errors. Every canvas action has a button (Bump the ice, Add charge, Spark!, Heat the air, three 'Thunder is' answers, Flash!, four distance answers, four places), and the canvas aria-label is rewritten after each action with the bump count, charge, strike target, count in seconds and where each person went.
